text: Every lesson in this chapter has built toward one real tension: contain fast, or contain carefully. The fastest-looking option is sometimes the one that quietly destroys evidence you'll need later. Powering off a machine loses everything that only ever lived in volatile memory — running processes, connection state, decryption keys in active use — none of which survives a shutdown.

Not every incident needs forensic-grade preservation, but a larger category than you'd expect does: anything that might lead to legal action, regulatory breach-notification reporting, or a cyber insurance claim. Acting fast without preserving evidence can turn a clean 'nothing was accessed' determination into an unprovable 'we can't say what was accessed' — a materially worse position, legally and reputationally, than the extra time preservation would have cost.

The practice that resolves this is sequencing, not picking a side. Isolate first, not power off — the host stays live, cut off from the network, stopping the damage without losing memory. Then acquire a memory dump and disk image with proper forensic tooling, hash it, and log who captured it and when, before eradication or rebuild ever touches the machine.

That documented chain of custody matters because if the evidence ever faces outside scrutiny — a regulator, a court, an insurer — an undocumented gap can undermine the whole thing. Only after acquisition is complete does the team move into eradication and rebuild, which is exactly where the next chapter picks up.

A healthcare provider discovers a server holding patient records may have been accessed. Under HIPAA, they have to prove what happened. The team isolates the server rather than shutting it down, captures a hashed memory dump and disk image with a logged chain of custody, and only then rebuilds. Months later, when a regulator asks for proof of scope, the evidence still exists. Next up: eradication — removing the actual root cause.
